rationale: A wins because it is disciplined: three real angles, three different protagonists, and proof gaps stated without decorating them. Its strongest line, "Monzo returns to the US — this time renting a banking license instead of chasing one," turns the launch into a reportable regulatory-access story. B has good material, but it starts padding: "Monzo's Partner-Bank Deal: What the Regulatory Structure Enables — and Where It Stops" is mostly the first comeback/licensing angle wearing a different coat, and "That's Not Supposed to Be the Neobank Story" imports a sector narrative the update did not supply.
gaps_in_A: "then spent it on a second shot at America" overstates the facts. The update gives sequence, not causality or spending from profit.
"renting a banking license" is punchy but loose. Partner-bank arrangements are not literally license rental; a banking trade reporter may punish that shortcut.
It skips a possible consumer product/explainer angle around checking, budgeting tools, invite-only access, and the partner bank, though that angle would need product access to earn coverage.
gaps_in_B: "Monzo's Partner-Bank Deal: What the Regulatory Structure Enables — and Where It Stops" duplicates the first licensing comeback angle instead of earning its own slot.
"That's Not Supposed to Be the Neobank Story" relies on an unsupplied premise about neobank economics. Maybe true, but this exercise did not give that proof.
"whether that structure invites regulatory attention" invents a regulatory-risk hook without any supplied public signal.
The next step, "meanest-editor," is the wrong first move for raw angles. The founder needs proof triage and journalist-fit-check before drafting.
